title: KB vs KiB File Size Explained — Why Government Portals Reject 300 KB PDFs
metaDescription: Understand the technical difference between KB (1000 bytes) and KiB (1024 bytes). Learn why a 300 KB PDF shows valid in Windows Explorer but fails portal uploads.
author: Zcompressor Engineering
heroHeadline: KB vs KiB file size: why government portals reject 300 KB PDFs.
heroDescription: Ever compressed a file to exactly 300.0 KB according to Windows, only for a portal like UPSC or NSP to reject it for exceeding 300 KB? Here is the binary vs decimal calculation discrepancy.

sections.heading: Decimal KB (1,000 bytes) vs Binary KiB (1,024 bytes).
body: In international SI standards, 1 Kilobyte (KB) equals 1,000 Bytes. However, computer operating systems (like Windows Explorer) historically calculate 1 Kilobyte using binary math: 1 KiB = 1,024 Bytes.

If a government portal validates file limits using strict byte counts (e.g. 300 KB = 300,000 Bytes max), a file that measures 298 KiB in Windows Explorer actually contains 305,152 Bytes! To the portal server, your file is 305.15 KB—over the 300 KB limit—triggering an immediate rejection.

sections.heading: How Zcompressor prevents byte-count rejection.
body: Zcompressor measures PDF file sizes using strict decimal Byte calculations (1 KB = 1,000 Bytes). When you select a 300 KB target, Zcompressor ensures the resulting file contains less than 300,000 total Bytes, guaranteeing 100% acceptance across all portal validation engines.

faq.q: What is the safest target size for a 300 KB portal limit?
faq.a: Aiming for 280 KB – 290 KB ensures your document stays safely under both binary (KiB) and decimal (KB) verification checks.
